claims.text: At temperatures above approximately 700 °C, FeNiCrCoCu thin-film coatings develop an in situ oxide layer through tribo-oxidation.
The high-temperature oxide layer is continuous and adherent.
The oxide layer is a multi-component oxide that may contain spinel-type phases.
The oxide layer acts as both a protective barrier and a solid lubricant.
Formation of the oxide layer reduces overall wear rate and friction.
At lower temperatures, the protective oxide film does not form or remains discontinuous.
Wear is higher at lower temperatures than at approximately 800–900 °C.
The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating has a homogeneous solid-solution microstructure.
The as-deposited coating has no preformed oxide scale.
Annealing the coating in air promotes and accelerates protective oxide-scale formation.
Increasing wear-test temperature promotes and accelerates oxide-scale formation.
The tribo-oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The tribo-oxide film hinders further material removal.
Oxide-film formation changes wear to a less abrasive regime.
Tests above approximately 700 °C will exhibit lower wear depth than tests at room temperature or below 500 °C.
Tests above approximately 700 °C will exhibit a lower coefficient of friction than lower-temperature tests.
Post-test analysis will find a continuous oxide film at high temperature that is absent or discontinuous at lower temperatures.
The proposed protective mechanism requires an oxidizing atmosphere and may fail in inert or reducing atmospheres because oxide formation is suppressed.
Copper in FeNiCrCoCu may form comparatively less-adherent oxides.

contradictions.description: The intervention alternates between pre-oxidation and raising the test temperature, while the baseline simultaneously changes coating state and temperature. Moreover, the pre-oxidized samples tested at 500 °C may already possess an oxide film, conflicting with the general prediction that the film is absent or discontinuous at lower test temperatures.
